extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys/agents, and applicants drafting or prosecuting AI/ML-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for preparing, claiming, and prosecuting patent applications directed to AI/ML inventions across multiple jurisdictions, including ethical risk considerations, claim drafting, enablement, inventive_step assessment, and inventorship issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data usage, consent, and respect for privacy decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers, developers, and deployers of automated systems should notify and seek permission with regard to data usage, and respect decisions regarding collection, use, access, transfer, and deletion of private data in appropriate ways and to the greatest extent possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should provide clarity about user choices, and not obfuscate user choice or burden users with defaults that are privacy invasive. Consent requests should be brief and understandable. Enhanced protections and restrictions for data and inferences related to sensitive domains (e.g., health, work, education, criminal justice, and finance), and for data pertaining to youth, should only be used for necessary functions. Practice Tip: Be cautious about describing the types of data used in patent applications; broadening scope may implicate privacy laws (e.g., HIPAA). Avoid implications of unauthorized/unexpected data usage in filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and Explanation (transparency to affected users)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users should know why and how an AI system made its determination. People should understand that an automated system is being used and understand how and why the automated system contributes to outcomes that impact them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May require generally accessible plain language explanations, clear descriptions of overall system functioning and the role of automation, notice that such systems are in use, who is responsible for the system, and explanations of outcomes. People should timely receive notice as to how and why an outcome that impacts them was determined by an automated system. Practice Tip: Consider describing in the patent application that the user is notified of the AI decision and that AI is being used; inform clients of such guidance to mitigate future issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human alternatives, consideration, and fallback (opt-out and human review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated systems should provide people a choice to opt out of AI decision-making and have fallback access to a human if the system errs, fails, or the person wants to challenge a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated systems intended for sensitive domains (criminal justice, employment, education, health, etc.) should be tailored and incorporate human consideration for adverse or high‑risk decisions. Examples include wrongful fraud flags, medical denial due to data mix-ups, or automated firing without human review. Practice Tip: While patenting an AI system typically does not require disclosing an opt-out feature, practitioners should advise clients about potential harms from error-prone personal data and may recommend adding embodiments that allow individuals to contact a human or operator to dispute outputs; such embodiments, though likely not patentable, may be favorably viewed publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: G7 Code of Conduct (voluntary lifecycle risk management and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The G7 adopted an 11‑point voluntary AI Code encouraging companies to ensure AI safety and dependability, identify/assess/mitigate risks across the AI lifecycle, confront post‑deployment misuse, and publish reports on capabilities, limitations, usage, and potential misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code emphasizes investing in robust security controls and public reporting. It is voluntary and largely directed at companies operating in G7 countries; patent practitioners should be aware of this broader ethical context when advising clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address ethical risk mitigation principles in patent drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Although ethical risk mitigation principles in the Blueprint are non‑binding, patent practitioners should address these principles with clients when preparing patent applications directed to AI systems that may raise ethical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice tips include adding features or embodiments that address high‑risk decisions, and including embodiments permitting human dispute or review. Doing so can help mitigate negative public or governmental sentiment even if such features are not patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO two‑hurdle approach to mathematical methods/AI
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO uses a two‑hurdle approach: (1) determine whether the claimed subject matter is excluded (e.g., a mathematical method per se), and (2) substantive examination to assess enablement, clarity, novelty, and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of any technical means (computer, network, internet) is often sufficient to overcome the first hurdle. The second hurdle addresses whether the disclosure is enabling and whether claims are clear, unitary, novel, and inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMVIK approach and treatment of non‑technical features (inventive step at EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step is assessed via the COMVIK/problem‑solution approach: assess differences from closest prior art and consider only those differences that contribute to the technical character for inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑technical features (mathematical methods, AI/ML algorithms per se) are often ignored unless, in context, they contribute to technical character by producing a technical effect. Technical contribution can arise from application to a field of technology or adaptation to specific technical implementation. Training steps (generating training set, training algorithm) may contribute if they support the technical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of application to a field of technology (EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application to a field of technology must be specific; a generic purpose (e.g., 'controlling a technical system') is insufficient. Claims should be functionally limited to the technical application and not encompass further non‑technical applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of technical contributions: controlling specific technical systems/processes (X‑ray, steel cooling), digital audio/image/video enhancement or analysis (de‑noising, feature detection), classifying digital images based on low‑level features, using a neural network in heart monitoring to identify irregular heartbeats. Examples of non‑technical purposes: classifying text documents by textual content or abstract data records without technical use indication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to a specific technical implementation can provide technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: AI/ML algorithms may contribute to technical character when adapted for a specific implementation or motivated by technical considerations of computer/network internal functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: algorithm design enabling efficient hardware implementation; using GPUs for training steps and CPUs for preparatory steps such that implementation contributes to the technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO case law constraints for ML inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: ML per se is often considered part of the trend of technology and thus obvious; an invention must specify more than just using ML and must solve a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems must be technical; ML designed with the functioning of the computer in mind may contribute (e.g., enabling or improving parallel processing). Improvements relied upon for inventive step must be present across all claimed embodiments, credible from the application content, and more than merely encoding/automating human expert knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting best practices for AI‑related European patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft separate claims for training and inference phases; make technical features in each phase the core of the claim so that the technical purpose and technical effect are evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient specific technical detail in the description (training data, training parameters, input data for inference, inference parameters) to enable the claimed invention. Disclose fallback positions in claim‑ready language (e.g., in summary) given restrictive EPO added‑matter rules. Even if not included in claims, disclose technical features that could serve as fallbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non‑technical terminology and show causal chain to technical effect in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid non‑technical terms (that may be associated with mathematical/business methods) in claims; ensure claim features form a causal chain leading to the asserted technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support the causal chain by ensuring interconnections/interactions between claim features are present and highlighted so the technical effect is clear to the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO enablement and disclosure requirements for AI inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Japan Patent Act Article 36 provisions, the detailed explanation must be clear and sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to work the invention; for AI‑applied inventions, the specification should demonstrate the capacity to create a learned model with a certain degree of accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is any relationship between input and output data in training data used to create the learned model, the specification should show that the AI algorithm can create a learned model that performs accurate estimation based on that relationship. Practice example (Case Example 49): failure to disclose correlations/support between alternative feature values and target variables can render the application non‑compliant with support/enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA claim evaluation as a whole and inventive step via algorithm adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: China's CNIPA requires considering the claim as a whole; technical features, algorithms, business rules, and process steps should not be evaluated separately. Algorithm adjustments that differ from existing technology may support inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claimed solution that enables a CNN to process images of various sizes (solving a technical problem) can be patentable. Section 9.6 clarifies examination of algorithmic/business rule features together with practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA written description requirements for AI/biz‑rule inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should clearly provide technical features supporting and interacting with each other in their functionality to solve a technical problem; algorithms should be combined with practical application (include at least one input parameter and at least one output related to the specific technology area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For business rules/method features, include detailed explanations of the entire process of how the technical problem is solved. If improvements to user experience are objective, the specification should show how these are implemented using technical features and how features interact to generate such effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean approach to AI patent eligibility and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Korea identifies patentable subject matter based on novelty and inventiveness if technical ideas are embodied in a computer; a technical idea within a general‑purpose computer may suffice if software and hardware operate together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some subject matter (economic laws, mathematical formula, mental activity) remains unpatentable if lacking software/hardware integration or technical idea. Enablement may require description of relationships between input and output data from a trained model, including learning data, correlations to solutions of a technical problem, and how a trained model is generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK exclusions and positive treatment for specific technical AI applications
rubrics_metrics.description: UK Patents Act exclusions (discovery, mathematical method, computer program, presentation of information, schemes/rules) apply 'to the extent' the application relates to that thing as such; UK practice interprets exclusions narrowly since 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims functionally limited to a specific technical application of AI/ML can be patentable; abstract mathematical methods and non‑technical business method applications will be refused. Include within the application inputs, training, outputs, technical applications, interactions with physical systems outside the computer, and detailed system/software architecture for sufficiency. Recent case law (Emotional Perception AI v Comptroller‑General) found an ANN/training could produce a technical effect (external technical effect) that contributes to patentability; UKIPO updated practice to reflect that ANNs should not be objected under the 'program for a computer' exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of training and architecture details for sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency (enablement) requires detailed disclosure related to training of ANNs and system architecture when training is relied upon as the point of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UKIPO endorsed EPO Board decision T161/18 criticizing lack of detailed disclosure related to ANN training; include training detail in specification to avoid insufficiency refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI inventorship and conception standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship rests on who conceived the invention: conception is the complete performance of the mental part of the inventive act — formation of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as applied in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI is merely a tool used by humans, the human(s) who contributed to conception (designing architecture, choosing input data, developing algorithms) are inventors. However, scenarios with minimal human involvement raise questions whether any human qualifies as an inventor. Under most current patent laws, AI cannot be listed as an inventor. Practice: counsel clients about inventorship issues and document human contributions. Consider jurisdictional differences when advising clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: US position on AI inventorship (statutory/national practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. law and practice (MPEP, Federal Circuit) interpret 'inventor'/'individual' to require natural persons; AI cannot be named as an inventor under current law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO has solicited comments (2019, 2023) on AI and inventorship but has not changed the requirement. Court decisions (Thaler applications) and Federal Circuit affirmed that inventors must be natural persons; Supreme Court denied certiorari. Practitioners should list natural persons who contributed to conception and be aware of ongoing policy discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: International variability on AI inventorship (jurisdictional outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions differ: South Africa has allowed a patent listing AI as inventor (practical concerns noted), while many others (EPO, Australia ultimately on appeal, U.S.) have rejected AI as inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South Africa's grant may reflect that its substantive examination is limited to formalities. Australia had initial favorable decision but higher courts ruled against AI inventor claims; EPO Legal Board and many national offices reject AI inventorship. Practitioners should track jurisdictional developments and plan filings/assignments accordingly.
